body.text: Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts, also known as Aerodrome Forecasts, are prepared by Aerodrome Forecast Office (AFO).
The definition of terminal is an area within five 8 km of the center of an airport’s runway complex.
A TAF will consist of expected meteorological conditions significant to aviation at the airport (terminal) for a specified time period.
TAFs are a critical element of aviation weather services because they are a key product in decisions on aircraft movement.

slides.title: Use of Vicinity (VC)

body.text: Used in combination with fog (FG), showers (SH), and thunderstorms (TS)
Less stringent operational impacts on users than PROB30 groups
Vicinity =  A donut-shaped area between circles with radii of 5 and
10 SM from the center of the runway complex of an airport.

slides.notes:
--When the Forecaster feels there is a less than 50% chance for significant weather within the terminal aerodrome…but still wants to make the user aware of the potential for fog, showers, or thunderstorms w/in the airfield…he/she may chose to include a Vicinity in the TAF.

--The use of VC has less stringent operational impact on the users than PROB30 or TEMPO. Basically, with a PROB30 or TEMPO…the user has to treat this as the prevailing condition…meaning Commercial airlines might add extra fuel for an alternate destination…or for the GA Pilot, this could mean you are grounded depending on your flight credentials and/or aircraft capabilities.
 
--What does it mean if you, the TAF user, see a VC or a CB in the TAF? Even though the prevailing wx conditions are not show stoppers, the user needs to be pro-active and ask himself “what will I do if I encounter TS within the vicinity of the Airfield? Will this cause me significant problems…or can I (and my aircraft) handle this? 

--As for CB…the user will need to treat this as a heads up that the atmosphere they are flying into/out of is unstable…which could mean turbulence…or even an isolated thunderstorm or two might pop up…but the forecaster confidence is low…and if Tstorms do develop, they will be short-lived and minimal in coverage.

slides.title: TAF Writing Philosophy

body.text: Through the TAF, Forecasters have a great opportunity
to enhance flight safety and save customers both time and money.

slides.notes: Over the past several years…the outreach efforts and forecast verification have indicated that although spectrum of TAF user and aviation customers is great, there are a few common needs throughout these groups…the need for CLEAR, CONCISE, CONSISTENT, RELEVENT, TIMELY, & ACCURATE TAFs—ref: Distance Aviation Learning Courses (DLAC)

slides.title: Forecaster Best Practices

body.text: Goal: Avoid writing the un-amendable, ambiguous TAF and strive
for an effective, practical, user-friendly TAF by…
Establishing trends and writing to Aviation Flight Categories first
Add detail to the first 6 hours of the TAF, known as the critical TAF period
Limit the use of PROB groups

slides.notes:
--In the past couple years, Forecasters have had a sort of paradigm shift…where we are no longer writing the un-amendable TAF…meaning we are no longer throwing in everything but the kitchen sink. In the process, we’ve had to Find a way to provide quality service to our customers and present the realm of possibilities while avoiding the ‘cry wolf syndrome’ (reducing our FAR). 
How do the forecasters indicate the threat for weather, thunderstorms for example, when the probability is less than 50%?? 
--Best Practices say to limit the use of TEMPO (which is for probability greater than 50% anyway) and avoid the use of PROB30? 
--What about the use of CB and/or VC?

body.text: No more than 5 lines per TAF
Link similar visibility and ceilings into similar categories (scenario forecasting)
Mention cirrus only when that’s all there is to mention
Consider the local critical thresholds for the airport
At least get the forecast category (VFR, IFR) correct
Focus on the aviation critical weather—spend most of your energy on the forecast period that is expected to be below VFR
If you can’t get exact numbers, at least show the trend
Limit your use of conditional groups—don’t hedge, make a decision!
When you do use a TEMPO group, try not to jump more than one category (e.g., from VFR to CAT II)

slides.title: Volcanic AshAviation Seminar, AlanyaIan Mills

body.text: Approximately 15-25 volcanoes each year world-wide erupt volcanic ash to jet aircraft cruising levels
Radar systems on jet aircraft cannot detect volcanic ash
Damage to outer frame due to abrasion by ash particles → expensive repairs
Ash melts at high operating temperatures of jet engines → can stall engines
Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres (VAACs) issue volcanic ash advisory statements
Requirement for detection and monitoring of eruptions/ash clouds
Set up in early 1980’s in response to incidents where aircraft lost power in one or more engines

June 1982 a British Airways 747 lost all four engines and suffered severe damage on encountering volcanic ash over Indonesia.  The aircraft descended to 12,000ft before being able to restart some engines and make an emergency landing in Jakarta.
London VAAC runs an atmospheric dispersion model (NAME) to forecast the plume behaviour.

slides.notes:
The motivation for this developmental work is two-fold: 
There is a need for improved volcanic ash detection tools, and
We have the opportunity to develop them using Meteosat Second Generation data.

The need for new, improved tools is to improve the existing VAAC service – there are limitations with existing observations of ash and this development will reduce these limitations.
The need to maintain our status as a VAAC – to show the outside world that we do take our responsibility seriously and provide the best service possible with current technology. I have attended a couple of international meetings about the use of satellite data and it has been commented upon on more than one occasion that very little resources are used to provide the tools and personnel for the London VAAC.
The opportunity that we have is to try to make the best use of newly available MSG data. These data are operationally available in the next couple of weeks and are routinely received and used in the Met Office. MSG will replace Meteosat – currently our main operational geostationary satellite and our major source of satellite imagery. MSG is superior to Meteosat in many ways …
